title: Single-Producer/Single-Consumer Ring Buffer
statement:
A circular buffer between a producer and a consumer -- an ISR filling it, a
task draining it, or just two halves of a driver -- needs `push` and `pop`
that never move data through a lock. The hard part is not the wraparound
arithmetic. It is telling **full** apart from **empty** when both leave the
buffer's two indices pointing at the same slot.

This exercise uses the standard fix: **the buffer always leaves one slot
unused**. A buffer of `capacity` N holds at most `N - 1` items. In exchange,
`head == tail` means empty and nothing else, and `(head + 1) % capacity ==
tail` means full and nothing else -- no separate count to keep in step with
the indices, and no ambiguity.

## Your functions

```
int ring_push(int *buf, int capacity, int *head, int *tail, int value);
int ring_pop(int *buf, int capacity, int *head, int *tail, int *value_out);
```

`buf` is the backing array, `capacity` its size, `*head` and `*tail` the
running indices -- read them, and if you accept the operation, advance them
modulo `capacity` and write through the pointers.

- `ring_push` stores `value` at `*head` and returns `1` if there was room;
  if the buffer is full, it changes nothing and returns `0`.
- `ring_pop` reads the oldest value into `*value_out` and returns `1` if
  there was one; if the buffer is empty, it leaves `*value_out` untouched and
  returns `0`.

## Watch out

- **A buffer of capacity N really does hold only N - 1 items.** Push N times
  into a fresh buffer and the last push must report full, not succeed. This
  is not a bug to route around -- it is the mechanism that makes `head ==
  tail` unambiguous, and it is exactly what the fixed tests check.
- Advance the index **after** using it, both directions: `ring_push` writes
  to the current `*head` and then moves `*head` on; `ring_pop` reads from the
  current `*tail` and then moves `*tail` on. Get the order backwards and the
  first push or pop silently touches the wrong slot.
- `% capacity` wraps an index from `capacity - 1` back to `0`. There is no
  guarantee `capacity` is a power of two, so a bitmask shortcut is not
  available here -- use the modulo.

tests.name: a capacity-3 buffer holds only 2 items
tests.stdin:
3
PUSH 1
PUSH 2
PUSH 3
POP
PUSH 4
PUSH 5
POP
POP
POP
POP
tests.expected_stdout:
OK
OK
FULL
POP 1
OK
FULL
POP 2
POP 4
EMPTY
EMPTY
tests.description: The third PUSH must report FULL before anything is popped -- capacity 3 holds at most 2 items.

tests.name: filling a buffer to exactly capacity - 1
tests.description: Capacity 4 holds 3 items; the 4th push is the one that must fail.
